edits.new: - Optical energy per point for OPA lidars is 1,360–1,700 nJ in Pointcloud's comparison table [S]. The 1,360 nJ is that of Jilin University's 128-channel OPA (Li *et al.*, *Photon. Res.* 2021) at 100 m on a 90% target, and the 1,700 nJ that of the 8,192-element array at 35 m on a 10% target. The table counts energy per pulse or per up-and-down chirp pair, and Li *et al.*'s 26 dBm input, less its 17.7 dB system insertion loss, over $2\times100$ µs of chirp gives the same figure [E: $398\ {\rm mW}\times10^{-1.77}=6.8$ mW and $6.8\ {\rm mW}\times200\ \mu{\rm s}=1.35\ \mu{\rm J}$]. Pointcloud's FPA uses 46 nJ (at 65 m and 30%), and the 512-pixel coherent receiver array of Rogers et al. (*Nature* 2021, §C10.4) 212 nJ, from the same table [S].

edits.old: DTU's 120-element array spread over 6 mm has a *simulated* main-lobe fraction of 0.8%. Its *measured* floor, only 3–6 dB below the peak, was recorded with a camera of 0.13° resolution, whose pixels each integrate many sidelobe spots of width $\lambda/D$, with $D=6$ mm the aperture: $1.55\ \mu{\rm m}/6\ {\rm mm}=2.6\times10^{-4}$ rad $=0.015^\circ$, about $0.13/0.015\approx9$ spots per pixel along that axis. A pixel's floor therefore sits far above the per-spot mean of §C10.1, $1/N=1/120$, i.e. −21 dB [E].
edits.new: DTU's 120-element array is one aperiodic row of 120 grating emitters at a mean pitch of about 50 µm across 6 mm, each grating 5 mm long and steered by wavelength along the other axis, so it is sparse along one axis only [P]. Its *simulated* main-lobe fraction of 0.8% comes from the array factor alone, with a flat element pattern over the ±90° field, and it is what §C10.1 predicts: counting spots in angle as the paper does, $N_{\rm spot}=\pi D/\lambda=\pi\times6\ {\rm mm}/1.55\ \mu{\rm m}\approx12{,}200$ (the paper's ≈12,000 simulated resolvable points), so $N/N_{\rm spot}=120/12{,}200=1.0\%$, and random 120-element layouts give 0.9% [E]. Its *measured* floor, only 3–6 dB below the peak, is set mostly by the camera's 0.13° resolution, about 9 main-lobe widths ($\lambda/D=1.55\ \mu{\rm m}/6\ {\rm mm}=2.6\times10^{-4}$ rad $=0.015^\circ$, with $D=6$ mm the aperture). The camera spreads the main lobe over those 9 widths and reads its peak about 9.5 dB low ($10\log_{10}9$), while it averages the floor to its mean, $1/N=1/120$ of the true peak (−21 dB). The observed peak therefore stands only about 11 dB above the mean floor, and the floor's highest points lie about 5–6 dB above that mean, so only about 4–6.5 dB below the observed peak, close to the measured 3–6 dB [E: 20 layouts of 120 random emitters over 6 mm with exact amplitudes, seen through a 0.13° Gaussian response, give 11 dB from the observed peak to the mean floor and 4–6.5 dB to the floor's highest point]. The paper itself attributes the gap from its simulated 12.8 dB to amplitude variation in its cascaded directional couplers [P].
edits.why: Source found by the R5_C10_part1 research agent; see sources/R5_C10_part1_findings.md, R5_C10_part1-02.

edits.old: - A Monte Carlo check with random sparse arrays gave **8.5%** main-lobe power for $N=128$ and $N_{\rm spot}\approx1{,}140$ ($N/N_{\rm spot}=11\%$), with a peak sidelobe of −11 dB and a mean sidelobe of −21 dB. For $N=256$ and $N_{\rm spot}\approx1{,}720$ ($N/N_{\rm spot}=15\%$) it gave 12%, −12.6 dB and −24 dB.
edits.new: - A Monte Carlo check [E] placed $N$ isotropic elements independently and uniformly at random over an aperture $L=N_{\rm spot}\lambda/2$: $570\lambda=0.88$ mm for $N=128$ and $N_{\rm spot}=1{,}140$, and $860\lambda=1.33$ mm for $N=256$ and $N_{\rm spot}=1{,}720$, at 1.55 µm. It evaluated the far field over all of visible space, $\sin\theta$ from −1 to 1, which holds $N_{\rm spot}=2L/\lambda$ beamwidths, and counted the main lobe out to its first nulls, $|\sin\theta|<\lambda/L$. Over 200 trials it gave **9.2%** main-lobe power for $N=128$ ($N/N_{\rm spot}=11\%$), with a peak sidelobe of −11.5 dB and a mean sidelobe of −21 dB, and 11.8% ($N/N_{\rm spot}=15\%$), −13.0 dB and −24 dB for $N=256$. Both fractions match the expectation $0.90\,N/(N_{\rm spot}+N)$, 9.1% and 11.7%: 90% of the main lobe lies inside its first nulls, and the main lobe's own power adds to the total.

edits.old: - Waveguide-width errors, correlated along each guide, accumulate phase at about 12 rad per nm of width error per mm of Si path, so after a few millimetres the uncalibrated phases are effectively random. The Si phase-coherence length, the guide length beyond which two nominally identical paths no longer keep a predictable phase relation, is about 1.6–4 mm [I].
edits.new: - Waveguide-width errors, correlated along each guide, accumulate a phase $(2\pi/\lambda)(\partial n_{\rm eff}/\partial w)$ per unit width error and length: about 12 rad per nm of width error per mm for a 400 nm wide Si strip ($\partial n_{\rm eff}/\partial w=3\times10^{-3}\ {\rm nm^{-1}}$ at 1,550 nm, Rizzo *et al.*, *Opt. Lett.* 2023) and about 6.5 rad for the common 500 nm strip ($1.6\times10^{-3}\ {\rm nm^{-1}}$, Yang *et al.*, *Opt. Express* 2015) [I; $(2\pi/1.55\ \mu{\rm m})\times3\times10^{-3}\ {\rm nm^{-1}}\times1\ {\rm mm}=12$ rad]. After a few millimetres the uncalibrated phases are therefore effectively random. Yang *et al.* measured the phase-coherence length of 220 nm SOI waveguides, the length $L_{\rm coh}$ at which the random phase reaches an rms of $\sqrt2$ rad (its rms is $\sqrt{2L/L_{\rm coh}}$ for a length $L$, so $\langle e^{i\Delta\phi}\rangle=e^{-1}$ at $L_{\rm coh}$), at 4.2 mm for strip and 1.6 mm for rib waveguides, from 800 Mach–Zehnder interferometers across one 6-inch foundry wafer [I].
edits.why: Source found by the R5_C10_part1 research agent; see sources/R5_C10_part1_findings.md, R5_C10_part1-05.

edits.old: Published 2D arrays are orders of magnitude smaller [U].
edits.new: The largest integrated 2D phased arrays with a phase control per element found for this report are far smaller: 128 emitters in a waveguide-fed silicon chip (Fatemi *et al.*, *IEEE JSSC* 2019) and 160 × 160 = 25,600 MEMS-actuated grating phase shifters in a free-space-fed chip with a 6.6° × 4.4° field (Wang *et al.*, *Optica* 2019) [I], about 9,400 and 47 times fewer ($1.2\times10^{6}/128$ and $1.2\times10^{6}/25{,}600$). Liquid-crystal-on-silicon modulators have millions of phase pixels but respond in milliseconds [I, as cited by Wang *et al.*].
